newsitem.title: GERMANY: Waigel blames opposition SPD for German budget woes.
newsitem.headline: Waigel blames opposition SPD for German budget woes.

text.p: German Finance Minister Theo Waigel blamed the opposition Social Democrats on Friday for blocking the government's reform efforts and then urged the left-leaning party to cooperate on plans to cut taxes and unemployment.

Defending the government's policies at a special session of parliament on Friday, Waigel officially informed parliament that tax revenues for 1997 would be 18 billion marks ($10.6 billion) less than expected.
The tax shortfall, which he first announced at a news conference on Thursday, creates a hole that will make it hard for Germany to qualify for the single European currency.

Waigel told the deputies that tax revenues were down because of low inflation, increased efforts by Germans to cut their taxes and schemes by companies to shift a greater portion of their profits abroad.
"The SPD has done nothing but torpedo our efforts to reform. You block everything we do," he said.
On Thursday Waigel said he wanted to revalue Bundesbank gold reserves and accelerate the pace of privatisation to fill the gaps.

Waigel then urged the SPD, which controls the upper house of parliament, to return to the negotiating table to work out a tax reform plan. Talks on a sweeping tax reform programme with the SPD collapsed earlier last month.
"You left because you were not ready for compromise," he said. "If you were interested in helping the unemployed, we could have an agreement within days."
Waigel said the problems, in particular the high unemployment levels, could be best resolved if the SPD cooperated with the government on a tax reform programme.
"We will not let anyone knock us off our concept for the urgently needed reforms," Waigel said. "We will stick with our policies to promote growth and overcome the current problems."
Wolfgang Schaeuble, parliamentary group leader of the ruling Christian Democrats (CDU), also urged the SPD to stop using their blockade through the upper house of parliament.
"I appeal on you to stop the blockade," Schaeuble said. "There is no reason to be afraid."
SPD parliamentary group leader Rudolf Scharping said it was astonishing that the government was blaming everyone but itself for the budget holes.

"The hole is so big now that the whole coalition could fit in there," Scharping said. "You have irresponsibly clouded the issues. You have no concept. You blame everyone else. You have lousy excuses for everything."

He blasted Waigel for damaging Germany's reputation with the Bundesbank gold plan. 'You have harmed Germany's standing and are now going about your way to harm our standing in international markets," he said. "It is irresponsible."

Ingrid Matthaeus-Maier of the SPD urged Kohl to fire Waigel for budgetary gimmicks that were harming Germany. "He is the minister of tax lies, the minister of high taxes and chaotic tax laws," she said.
Matthaeus-Maier said Waigel's plans to revalue gold and sell the government's shares in Deutsche Telekom AG before 2000 were having a devastating effect on the Germany's image abroad and in markets.
"Can you imagine how the CDU would react if a SPD government ever said it wanted to get its hands on Bundesbank gold?" she said. "You would be jumping off the roof of parliament."
Gregor Gysi, head of the reformed communist Party of Democratic Socialism (PDS), warned that revaluing gold would amount to printing new money.
"I can tell you from my experience in East Germany that as soon as the government started printing money there it was finished," Gysi said. ($ = 1.702 German Marks)
